lesson_3.title: The Hidden Cost of Removal
task: High-level languages provide built-in blocks to delete items, but you must understand their hidden algorithmic cost.
When you use a 'remove' command, the computer secretly runs an O(n) search to find the item, and then runs another O(n) loop to physically shift all remaining memory to the left to close the gap!
2. Use an 'If' block to check if the `target` is in the list using the `is in` block. (Remember: this is a hidden O(n) search!).
3. If it is in the list, use the 'remove first occurrence of' block to delete it from `arr`. (Remember: this triggers a hidden O(n) memory shift!).

lesson_3.title: The Illusion of Speed: Built-In Functions
task: High-level programming languages provide built-in methods (like 'count') that appear to execute instantly. This is a deliberate illusion.

Under the hood, the system is still executing a full O(n) linear loop, usually written in a lower-level language (like C or C++). You must understand that utilizing this block still incurs an O(n) computational cost.
2. Open the 'Lists' tab and utilize the built-in 'count occurrences of' block to find your `target`.
4. Algorithmic Takeaway: Even when you do not manually write the loop, you must mentally account for its O(n) time complexity when analyzing your program's efficiency.

lesson_4.title: Is the List in Order?
task: An array is 'sorted' if every number is smaller than or equal to the number right next to it.
To check this, we need to compare `arr[i]` with its right neighbor `arr[i+1]`. However, this introduces a classic algorithmic trap: The 'Index Out of Bounds' error!
2. First, handle the base cases: if the list has 1 or 0 items, return `True` (it's already sorted!).
3. Loop Boundaries: Create a 'count with i' loop. Set it to start at `0` and end at the length of the list MINUS 2.
-> Algorithmic Insight: Why length minus 2? Because if we go to the absolute last index, there is no `arr[i+1]` to check against, and the program will crash!
4. Inside the loop, check: If `arr[i]` is strictly GREATER than `arr[i+1]`, the order is broken! Return `False` immediately.
5. If the loop finishes checking every pair successfully, return `True` at the very end.

lesson_4.title: Defensive Slicing
task: Slicing allows you to extract a specific sub-section of an array.

However, hardcoding a slice from index 1 to 3 is a dangerous algorithmic trap! If the array only contains 2 items, your program will crash. We must use Defensive Programming to verify our boundaries first.
2. Defensive Boundary Check: Open the 'Logic' tab and use an 'If' block. If the length of `arr` is less than 4, return an empty list `[]` immediately to prevent a crash.
3. If the array is safely long enough, open the 'Lists (Built-in Type)' tab and grab the 'slice list' block.
4. Set the start index to `1` and the end index to `3`.

lesson_4.title: Memory Shift: Inserting at the Front
task: Adding an item to the END of a list (`append`) is incredibly fast because there is empty space waiting. This takes O(1) constant time.

However, squeezing an item into the FRONT of a list is an algorithmic bottleneck. The computer must physically shift every existing item one space to the right in memory to make room. This takes O(n) linear time!
2. Use the built-in 'insert at index' command to place your `item` variable at index `0` of the `arr`.
4. Algorithmic Takeaway: Although it looks like a single block of code, remember that the computer is secretly running an O(n) loop behind the scenes to shift the data!
